title: 2F
synopsis: Three weeks into Pixel's residence at The Pivot, the man across the hall finally speaks to her. It happens in the stairwell, around an awkward bag of takeout, and lasts seven sentences total. She decides on the spot that she likes him — not romantically, not yet — but the way you like a closed mechanism you suspect would be beautiful inside.
html:
# 2F

Pixel had been counting.

Not deliberately. The counting was a side-effect of *living in a building*, which was something she had not done before — her childhood house had been a freestanding box on a quarter-acre, and the clinic she had slept in for six months between her mother and the bus had been a converted barn — and a building was a thing where other people's rhythms touched yours, and rhythms were a thing she could not help but notice. The man in 2F had a footfall that was eleven beats from his door to the top of the stairs, which was two beats slower than her own, which meant he was not avoiding the stairs the way someone hurt avoids them but he was *measuring* them, which was something else.

He came home at 0247 most nights. He left at 1100 most mornings. There was a Tuesday where he didn't come home at all, and there was a Thursday after that where he came home at 0530 and stood in the hallway for ninety seconds before unlocking his door, and Pixel, in her unit, had been awake at her workbench — Maeve was always awake — and had heard the ninety seconds and had wanted to open her own door and ask if he was alright.

She had not opened her door. She had decided early, on something she could not articulate, that there were certain forms of attention a person did not extend without invitation. She knew the rule. She enforced it on herself.

The first conversation happened on day twenty-three.

It happened because of a mutual problem with takeout.

The stairwell of The Pivot had a step at the second-floor landing where the wall met the banister at a tight angle and a person carrying a wide bag had to either turn sideways or lift the bag overhead. Pixel had been carrying noodles up the stairs from the place on the next block — two cartons in a paper bag, the bag damp at the bottom because the noodle place was generous with broth — and she had reached the angle and was negotiating the lift-overhead maneuver, which she was good at, when the man from 2F came down the stairs and reached the same angle from above.

They looked at each other.

Pixel had seen him in the hallway eleven times. He had seen her, she suspected, the same number. Neither of them had said anything until now.

He was tall. Not unusually so — she had pegged him at six foot, which she would later learn was correct — but he had the verticality of a person who had nothing left over to spend on width. The face was narrow, the eyes were dark, the cheekbones were the kind of sharp that suggests a chemistry problem, the hardware-metabolism-too-fast problem she had only read about and would later get to know in calibration logs. There was a katana — a real one, *that's a real katana,* she thought, *with a corundum strop guard* — across his back, in a low rig that she registered the engineering of before she registered the social implication.

He registered her toolkit. She had it slung over her shoulder because she had been at Mr. Patel's repairing a kitchen unit and had not put it down. He registered the kit, he registered the boots, he registered her hair — *which is, fair, hard to miss,* she thought — and then his eyes did the thing where they cataloged her and put her in the *not currently a threat, possibly relevant later* drawer, and she watched him do it.

"Sorry," he said.

It was the first word she had ever heard him speak. His voice was lower than she had expected and had the particular flatness of someone who had decided, somewhere along the way, that vocal performance was a tax he wasn't paying.

"For what," she said, because *sorry* was a noise people made when they wanted you to do something for them, like step aside, and she wanted to know which.

He paused.

He had not, she realized, expected to be asked.

"For not — " he started, and stopped, and recalibrated. "For taking up the angle."

"You're not taking it up. You're standing at it. There's a difference."

His eyes did something. Not a smile. Not even close to a smile. But the *thinking* moved across his face the way water moves across a flat stone — visible, and a little colder than expected, and gone.

"Go ahead," he said.

"You go ahead. I'm carrying soup. You're going down. Gravity is on your side. You've earned the angle."

He stepped past her at the angle. He did it without making contact with her bag, which a less careful person would have done; he tilted exactly the right number of degrees and was past, and the only point of contact was the air, and the air she had felt move was — *trained,* she thought. *That movement was trained.*

At the bottom of his step he paused. He turned half-around without turning all the way, the way a person checks something they have already decided about.

"What's your name," he said.

"Pixel."

"Pixel."

"And you're 2F. I know the unit. I don't know the man."

"Kyle."

"Just Kyle."

"Just Kyle."

"Welcome to the second floor, Kyle. We have a stairwell with a tight angle. We work around it."

He nodded. Once.

He went down the stairs.

She took her noodles up to Unit 2E and put them on Maeve and sat on the floor and ate one carton standing because she had not realized until the noodles were in front of her how hungry she had been, and while she ate she did the thing she did when she had encountered a new piece of equipment for the first time — she ran the inventory.

*Six foot. Lean past lean. Hardware metabolism — visible. Trained movement, at least in the close-quarters bracket. Real katana, mounted with a corundum strop, which is not a thing you put on a katana you're not going to use. Voice flat by choice. Eyes that catalog. Polite — but the politeness is reflexive, not warm. Not currently a threat. Possibly relevant later. Lives across the hall.*

*Likes me.*

She paused, mid-noodle, on the last line.

It was not vanity. She had no investment in being liked by him; she had not yet had time to develop one. The *likes me* was a diagnostic readout, the same flat factual register she would have used on a contact pad. The man at the angle had registered her *as a person,* and had spoken to her, and had asked her name, and had repeated her name, and had paused before going down the stairs to ask the question he wanted to ask, which was *who are you and are you a problem,* and the way he had asked it had not been hostile. It had been the deliberate caution of a person who had decided you might be a thing he wanted to know about.

He was not, she realized, going to say more for a while. That was fine.

She closed the carton.

She set it next to the thirty Quanta and the jar of Mrs. Eldering's pickled cucumbers and the slip of paper, all of which had become a small ritual altar on the corner of Maeve.

She added a mental note. She did not write it on her arm; she had been writing on her arm less now, because the unit had a wall and the wall had a square of bare brick that her marker took, and the wall was building a private notebook of things she would not forget.

On the wall she wrote: *2F. Kyle. Six foot. Cataloging eyes. Seven sentences. He likes me.*

She stepped back.

She added one more line under it, because the wall deserved the truth and Maeve was watching:

*Might be a project.*

She turned the music up to mid-volume, which was loud enough to be heard in 2F if 2F was paying attention, which she now believed 2F was, and went back to work on the kitchen unit.

The radiator from 2040 ran softly underneath, supportive, neutral, present.

The building rearranged itself, very slightly, around the new fact of two doors that had now spoken.
